title: Passive and reflexive stems

objectives.can: Recognise the Peil, the Hithpeel and Hithpaal, and the Hophal.

explanation.summary: Beside its active stems (Peal, Pael, Haphel and Aphel) Aramaic has stems in which the subject receives the action or acts on itself: the Peil, the Hithpeel and Hithpaal, and the Hophal. They are common in Daniel and Ezra: 'it was given', 'it was found', 'it will be built', 'they were gathered', 'he was brought in'.

sections.heading: Four passive and reflexive stems
body: An active verb has a doer: 'the king set it up'. A passive verb makes the receiver the subject: 'it was set up'. A reflexive verb makes the doer and the receiver the same: 'he set himself up'. Aramaic has no single passive stem. It has four, and each one is loosely attached to an active stem.

The Peil is the passive of the Peal. The Hithpeel is the reflexive or passive of the Peal. The Hithpaal is the reflexive or passive of the Pael. The Hophal is the passive of the Haphel. These pairings are the usual ones, not rules: a Hithpeel may be a true reflexive in one verb and a plain passive in another, and some verbs have only one of the pair in these texts.

The corpus holds 62 Peil forms, 50 Hithpeel, 33 Hithpaal and 12 Hophal. It also has a handful of forms (five in all) whose prefix begins with א and not ה; the corpus calls them the Ithpeel and the Ithpaal.

sections.heading: The Peil
body: The Peil is the quiet member of the family: it has no prefix. It differs from the Peal by a vowel i after the first root consonant. The perfect third person masculine singular is שְׁלִיחַ 'it was sent' and רְשִׁים 'it was inscribed'; the feminine singular ends in -ַת, as every perfect does: פְּרִיסַת 'it was divided', קְטִילַת 'it was slain', יְהִיבַת 'it was given'. The plural ends in -וּ: פְּתִיחוּ 'they were opened', קְרִיבוּ 'they approached'.

The same pattern is the Peal passive participle: it is used as an adjective and is made to agree with its noun, like דְּחִיל 'feared, fearful', דְּחִילָה (feminine) and פְּתִיחָן (feminine plural) 'open'. The corpus tags both the perfect and the passive participle as Peil. Learn to tell them apart by what is added at the end: a perfect has a perfect ending (-ַת, -וּ), an adjective-like participle has the endings of the noun (-ָה, -ָן, -ִין).

One form in the texts, תְּקִילְתָּה in Daniel 5:27, is tagged as an imperfect Peil. It has the ending -ְתָּ that other perfects of the second person have, and it means 'you have been weighed'. Many grammars parse it as a perfect. Treat the corpus label as the corpus's reading, and the ending as the clue to the sense.
The Peil is very often the verb of a short passive clause with no doer named: 'a hand was sent', 'a writing was inscribed'.

sections.heading: The Hithpeel and the Hithpaal
body: Both stems begin with the sound hith-. The perfect has הִתְ-: הִתְגְּזֶרֶת 'it was cut out', הִשְׁתְּכַח 'it was found'. In the imperfect the prefix becomes יִתְ- or תִּתְ- (the person letter and then תְ): יִתְעֲבֵד 'it will be done', תִּתְבְּנֵא 'it will be built', יִתְרְמֵא 'he will be cast'. In the participle the prefix is מִתְ-: מִתְבְּנֵא 'being built', מִתְעֲבֵד 'being done'.

The Hithpeel is built on the Peal. It has no doubling of the middle consonant. The Hithpaal is built on the Pael, so its middle consonant is doubled: compare the Hithpeel יִתְעֲבֵד with the Hithpaal יִצְטַבַּע 'it will be wet', where the ב is doubled. The doubling shows in מִתְכַּנְּשִׁין 'being gathered' and in מִתְקַטְּלִין 'being killed'. In a weak verb the doubling may be hidden, so the corpus label and the meaning are the safe guide.

Some small changes make these stems look strange. First, when the first root consonant is a sibilant (ש, ז, צ) it changes place with the ת of the prefix, or changes it. The root שְׁכַח 'find' gives הִשְׁתְּכַח, not a form that begins הִתְשׁ-: the ש comes first and the ת follows it. Second, a ז after the prefix turns the ת into ד: הִזְדְּמִנְתּוּן (root זְמַן). Third, a צ turns it into ט: יִצְטַבַּע (root צְבַע).

The corpus labels some Hithpeel participles 'participle' and others 'passive participle', so the label alone does not tell you whether the sense is passive: read the sentence. The tables of forms below show only what occurs as a bare word: for שְׁכַח they hold the third person alone, since the second person (וְהִשְׁתְּכַחַתְּ) occurs only with a prefix, and for עֲבַד the imperfect holds the third masculine singular and the second masculine plural; every other cell is empty because the texts do not have it.

The meaning is passive in many verbs: 'was found', 'will be built', 'will be made'. It is reflexive or intransitive in others: הִתְנַדַּבוּ 'they offered themselves willingly'. The same stem therefore does two jobs, and context decides between them.

sections.heading: The Ithpeel and the Ithpaal
body: A few forms have the prefix אִתְ- or אֶתְ- in place of הִתְ-. The corpus labels them the Ithpeel and the Ithpaal. The five forms in the texts are the Ithpeel אִתְגְּזֶרֶת, אֶתְעֲקַרָה and אֶתְכְּרִיַּת, and the Ithpaal אֶשְׁתַּנִּי and אִתְיָעַטוּ. They are the same stems as the Hithpeel and the Hithpaal. The only difference is the first letter of the prefix.

A good example is the stone of Daniel 2. In verse 34 the stone is said to be הִתְגְּזֶרֶת, and in verse 45 it is said to be אִתְגְּזֶרֶת. The two forms have the same sense, 'was cut out'. The first has ה and the second has א, and the corpus gives them two labels.

sections.heading: The Hophal
body: The Hophal is the passive of the Haphel. It has a prefix ה with an u-vowel, written הֻ-, הוּ- or הֳ-: הֻעַל 'he was brought in', הֳקִימַת 'it was set up', וְהוּבַד 'it was destroyed'. A few forms have an a-vowel after the ה (הָנְחַת 'he was brought down', הָתְקְנַת 'it was restored') and the Hophal of 'come' is written הֵיתָיוּ 'they were brought'.

All twelve Hophal forms in the texts are perfects. There is no Hophal imperfect or participle here: say so, and do not invent one. In the perfect, the Hophal has the same endings as the Peil: -ַת for the third person feminine singular (הֳקִימַת, הוּסְפַת) and -וּ for the plural (הֻעַלּוּ, הֵיתָיוּ).

The Hophal is easily confused with the Haphel. The Haphel perfect begins הֲ- or הַ- (הֲקֵים 'he set up'); the Hophal begins with a u-vowel (הֳקִימַת 'it was set up'). One adds a doer, the other takes it away.

misunderstandings: A prefix הִתְ- does not always mean 'reflexive'. In the Hithpeel it is often a plain passive ('it was found'). Read the sentence to see whether the subject acts or is acted on.
The Hophal is not the Haphel. The Haphel adds a doer ('he set up'); the Hophal makes the thing set up the subject ('it was set up').
A Peil perfect (קְטִילַת) is not a participle. Look at the ending: -ַת is the perfect, -ָה and -ָן belong to the participle.
The Hithpaal is not the Hithpeel with a doubled letter by accident. The doubling is the Pael pattern, and it separates the two stems.

deeper.heading: Why there is no one passive stem
body: Grammarians explain the Peil as an old internal passive, made by changing the vowels of the Peal and adding no prefix. The Hithpeel and Hithpaal came to carry the passive meaning for the Peal and the Pael as the old internal passives faded; the Hophal is the one old internal passive that is kept beside the Haphel. This is one reconstruction of the history. The learner's task is only to see the forms and their senses.

examples.analysis: A chain of passives about the first beast. מְּרִיטוּ (10) is a Peil perfect, third masculine plural: its wings 'were plucked'. וּנְטִילַת (12) is a Peil perfect, third feminine singular: it 'was lifted'. הֳקִימַת (18) is a Hophal perfect, third feminine singular: it 'was made to stand' (the passive of the causative stem). יְהִיב (21) is a Peil perfect, third masculine singular: a heart 'was given'. Peil and Hophal stand next to each other.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then was the king exceeding glad, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he had trusted in his God.

examples.analysis: וְהֻסַּק (10) is a Hophal perfect, third masculine singular: Daniel 'was taken up' from the den. Earlier in the verse the king commanded the Haphel infinitive לְהַנְסָקָה, 'to take up'. הִשְׁתְּכַח (17) is a Hithpeel perfect, third masculine singular, from שְׁכַח: no hurt 'was found' on him. The ש stands before the ת of the prefix.

quoted.english: Forasmuch as thou sawest that a stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver, and the gold; the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass hereafter; and the dream is certain, and the interpretation thereof sure.'

examples.analysis: אִתְגְּזֶרֶת is an Ithpeel perfect, third feminine singular: the stone 'was cut out' of the mountain. In Daniel 2:34 the same event is told with the Hithpeel form הִתְגְּזֶרֶת. The two stems have the same meaning, and the prefix אִתְ- is the only difference.

examples.analysis: הִזְדְּמִנְתּוּן (11) is a Hithpaal perfect, third masculine plural: they 'have agreed together'. The root is זְמַן, and the ז has changed the ת of the prefix to ד. יִשְׁתַּנֵּא (17) is a Hithpaal imperfect, third masculine singular, 'will change' or 'be changed': the ש of the root שְׁנָא has gone before the ת of the prefix, and the ת is doubled, because the Hithpaal has a doubled middle consonant.
